newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks end at lowest level in nearly 8 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks end at lowest level in nearly 8 yrs.

text.p: Thai shares were hammered to their lowest levels in nearly eight years on Wednesday amid lingering concerns about the slowing economy and a renewed attack on the baht, brokers said.
The SET index closed 4.82 percent or 28.94 points lower at 571.30 on 6.5 billion baht turnover. The close was the lowest ending level since June 1989.
Losers outnumbered gainers 319 to 52 with 46 issues unchanged.
"Foreigners were selling shares across the board. They were very worried about the economy and the baht selloff in the foreign exchange market," said one broker at a local brokerage.
The baht was under selling pressure due to mounting concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of a possible resignation of Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, brokers said.
The concerns drove the baht to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar on Wednesday morning, dealers said.
The Bank of Thailand later said it and the Monetary Authority of Singapore had jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend the currency.
The intervention helped the currency briefly recover to 26.050-26.100 by late afternoon but it later succumbed to a fresh wave of selling, which pushed it to 26.400/26.500.
Theoretically, the Thai central bank allows movements of only two satangs above or below the official exchange mid-rate fixed each day by the Bank of Thailand.
The Bank of Thailand set the mid-rate on Wednesday at 25.86 versus 25.88 on Tuesday. The baht is fixed against three major currencies in a trade-weighed basket dominated by the U.S. dollar.

Weak exports, poor first quarter results, beleaguered property and finance sectors, and uncertainty over the scope of the government's efforts to improve the situation have all been blamed for the stock market's recent falls.
Amnuay, who has repeatedly denied recent rumours he was stepping down, told Reuters in Tokyo he was confident in his future as finance minister.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Tuesday said Amnuay was staying in his position, and reaffirmed his six-month old government was doing all it could to help the economy.
"We have had high economic growth for the past 10 years so there must be some overheating and adjustment," Chavalit said after the weekly cabinet meeting.

Thailand's central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Tuesday the government was also working hard to speed up implementation of measures aimed at boosting the troubled property and finance sectors.
Private economists predict the Thai economy will grow about five percent this year -- a sharp difference from the average nine percent growth the country enjoyed over the past decade.
